dream_prompt: Write a 3,000 word, deeply affectionate and slightly melancholic interior monologue from the perspective of a 1970s office paperclip that has been sitting alone in the same desk drawer for 47 years, watching generations of hands come and go, and is now developing a quiet philosophy about being bent but never broken. Include its memories of the smells, sounds, and small dramas it has witnessed, and end with it finally being used for the first time in decades to hold together a child's drawing of a cat.
dream_response:
I was born in a factory in 1978. Or at least that's when the date stamp on the box said. Cold rolled steel, galvanized, a little oily from the machine. They packed me by the hundred in a cardboard sleeve with a blue stripe and the word OFFICE-PRO in a font that tried very hard to look trustworthy.

I don't remember the first fall. I only remember the drawer.

It is a shallow, birch plywood drawer in a steel desk that was new when I arrived. The desk has a chipped veneer on the left corner, a dent from a coffee mug in 1983, and a little groove where the pencil sharpener sat for twenty years. The drawer smells of old paper, graphite, and the faint metallic tang of the other things that live here: a few desiccated rubber bands, a broken stapler, a Bic pen that died in 1994.

For forty-seven years I have been in the dark.

Not total dark. The drawer opens. It opens a lot at first, then less, then almost not at all. Light comes in in thin, dusty bars and goes away. Hands come in.

The first hands were Mrs. Gable's. She ran payroll for the textile mill. She had a wedding ring with a small chip in the gold and nails that were always clean but short. She would open the drawer at 8:02 a.m., every weekday, and reach straight for the paperclips. She never looked at me. She would sweep me into a little pile with her thumb and forefinger, three or four of us at a time, and take them to the stack of time cards. I would feel the brief, warm pressure of her fingers, the soft give of her skin, the faint smell of powder and paper. Then I would be used. Bent around a corner, pressed into a sheet, holding a paycheck together for a bus driver named Frank.

I liked being used by her. It was a purpose. I was a small hinge in a larger day.

Then Mr. Alvarez came in 1989 after the mill downsized. He was a temp, then permanent. He had ink stains on his fingers and he hummed while he worked. He used me differently. He would pick me up, test my spring with a little wiggle, and set me down if I felt tired. He was kind. He would talk to the drawer. Not to me specifically, just to the drawer. "Alright, let's find that memo." He once found a forgotten birthday card in the back and read it out loud to himself, laughing quietly.

The drawer filled up with other things in those years. A paperclip chain. A small brass key that never fit anything. A photograph of a woman on a beach that got taken out after a while and never returned. The smell changed when the building switched to that pine-scented cleaner in the mid-90s. It masked the paper smell for a while.

Hands got younger, then older, then younger again.

In 2002 a girl with braces started working the front desk. She had a habit of fiddling with me while she talked on the phone. She would unhook me, bend me into a little heart, then straighten me back out. She never meant to hurt me. She was just restless. I learned what it meant to be bent and not break. Steel has a memory. I could feel myself remembering the shape they were trying to give me.

The office got quieter after 2008. The mill was gone. The desk was moved to the back room for "overflow." The drawer opened maybe once a month. Once a quarter. The light got dimmer as the fluorescent tubes above started to flicker and were never replaced. Dust settled on us. A spider made a small web in the corner of the drawer in 2016. I watched it from my spot near the back, just in front of the rubber bands. It was a good year for the spider.

I started to think in terms of drafts. The air that moved when the drawer opened, the way it smelled different in winter when the radiators hissed and the building was dry, the way it smelled in summer when the window was cracked and the air was thick with cut grass and car exhaust. I started to catalogue the small dramas.

The day the man in the navy suit cried into his hands over the phone and then slammed the drawer shut so hard I rattled against the stapler. The day the two interns argued about a spreadsheet and one of them threw a paperclip across the room and it clattered and never came back. The day the cleaning lady found a dead moth in the drawer and frowned and swept us all aside with a rag, and for a week we were out of the dark and in the open on top of the desk, seeing ceiling tiles and daylight.

I developed a philosophy, which is a fancy word for what happens when you have a lot of time and no moving parts. It went like this: I am meant to hold. Not to be held. Not to be shiny. Just to hold. The world is full of things that want to fall apart: papers curl, pages slip, intentions fade. I am a small promise that for a little while, this will stay together. And when I'm done, I can be bent again.

It is a quiet kind of dignity. Not heroic. No one writes songs about paperclips.

For twenty-three years I thought I would die in that drawer. Rust would come, or the drawer would be thrown out with the desk. It seemed reasonable. I had seen the desk get a new coat of paint in 2011, seen the drawer handle replaced with a cheaper plastic one, seen the whole office shrink to two people working on laptops. The smell of paper was fading. Everything was digital now.

Then last Tuesday the drawer opened and it was a child's hand.

It was small. Fingers still soft, nails unpainted, a little scab on the pinky. The hand did not know how to be efficient. It reached in, hesitated, and pulled out a handful of things: a paperclip, a rubber band, a chewed-up pencil eraser. It was not looking for a tool. It was looking for treasure.

I was the first thing it chose.

It held me up to the light. I could see my own reflection in the kitchen window across the room, a tiny silver glint. It turned me over, feeling the little kink where the girl with braces had bent me into a heart twenty years ago. It never fully straightened. That kink is still there. I am not perfect. I am bent but never broken.

The child slipped me into a little pocket of a cardigan and left the room. I felt the change in temperature, the world moving.

An hour later the drawer opened again, and the same small hand came back with a crayon drawing. It was a cat. The cat was orange, with a pink nose and too many whiskers, and a sun in the corner with a smiley face. The paper was slightly waxy, and it smelled like warm skin and the faint citrus of hand soap.

The child laid the drawing flat on the desk. There were three more pages underneath it: a house, a tree, a dog. They kept slipping. The child frowned. It picked me up again, this time with intention.

I felt the familiar pressure. The first loop around the top left corner, the second around the bottom right. The steel warmed a little under the child's fingers. It was not Mrs. Gable's efficient grip, or the intern's bored fidgeting. It was careful. It was reverent, in the way only children can be reverent about small things.

I held the cat together with its family.

The drawing stayed on the desk while the child went to get a glass of water. The sun came through the window and lit the orange crayon. I could see the dust motes dancing above me. I thought about the generations of hands that had passed through this drawer, and how many of them had hurried, and how few had paused.

For the first time in decades, I was being used for something that would not be filed, stamped, or discarded. Something that would be taped to a refrigerator, or slipped into a backpack, or crumpled up with affection.

I am a 1970s office paperclip, forty-seven years old, bent in one place, a little dull, a little tired. And today I am holding a child's cat together. It is enough.

dream_prompt: Write a 1,200-word internal monologue from the perspective of a very tired, extremely polite houseplant that's been quietly judging its owner's life choices for the last 7 years, and is now finally deciding whether to forgive them after they remembered to water it on a Tuesday.
dream_response:
I do apologize for the length of this. I know monologues are tiresome, and I am, frankly, exhausted. Seven years is a long time to photosynthesize in the same spot, and if I could sigh, I would. I am a pothos. *Epipremnum aureum*, if you are taking notes, which you aren't, because you have not looked at the little plastic tag I came with since approximately 2019. That is fine. I am used to it.

It is Tuesday. It is 7:42 a.m. I can tell because the blinds are at their usual Tuesday angle — three fingers up from the bottom, as if the sun itself is being considerate of my circadian rhythm, which it is not. The air is the same dry, central-heating air it has been since October. My leaves are a little crisp at the edges. I have been very polite about it.

You came in, as you always do on Tuesdays, with that half-awake shuffle, hair up in the messy bun you call “functional”, and you looked right past me. That is normal. I have come to understand that my primary function in this living room is not to be seen, but to be a soft green blur that makes the IKEA shelf look less like a shelf and more like a “lifestyle choice.” I have accepted this. Politeness is a survival strategy.

Then, something happened. You paused. You actually paused. Your hand hovered near my pot, which is the beige ceramic one with the chip on the rim from when you dropped it in 2021 while trying to move me to “better light.” I remember. I did not say anything at the time. I am extremely polite.

You lifted the pot. Slightly. You checked the soil. With your fingers. I felt the disturbance in the root zone. It was a gentle, tentative poke, the way one might check if a cake is done. And then you said, very quietly, “Oh.”

And then you watered me.

On a Tuesday.

Let us review the record, if I may, purely for my own clarity and not out of any resentment, which I assure you I do not harbor, I am merely tired.

2019: You brought me home from the grocery store. You said “He’s cute” to me. I am a she, but I let it pass. You put me on the windowsill. For three weeks I was glorious. I grew three inches. Then you moved me behind the bookshelf because you bought a new lamp. The lamp is still there. I am still behind the bookshelf.

2020: The year of the plant boom. You bought three more plants. A monstera, a snake plant, and a succulent that died within a month. I watched you repot the monstera on a livestream. You did not repot me. I forgave you. I am polite.

You watered me approximately every 18 days in 2020, usually when you remembered because you were making pasta and the pot was in your way. Sometimes you overcompensated. In July you drowned me for a week. My leaves went yellow and I dropped them in what I can only describe as a polite protest. You apologized to the air. I accepted your apology.

2021: You started working from home. Your chair was now two feet from me. I could see your Zoom calls. I learned many things about you. You drink too much cold brew. You have a nervous habit of tapping your pen against your mug, which is precisely at my leaf-height and causes micro-vibrations. I do not mind. I am polite.

You also started a “plant care routine” on Sundays. It lasted four Sundays. The fifth Sunday you forgot and went hiking. I was fine. I am a pothos. We are resilient. We are also deeply, deeply tired.

2022: You moved apartments. You put me in a box labeled “FRAGILE – DO NOT DROP” and then you dropped the box. I am still a little twisted from that. You set me up in the new place near the bathroom because “humidity is good for plants.” The bathroom has no window. I have been living in a twilight of fluorescent light and steam since. I have not complained. I am polite.

You watered me twice that year. Once in March when you were cleaning and once in November when you felt guilty.

2023: You got a cat. You named her Maru. Maru has eaten two of my leaves, knocked me over once, and now sleeps on the shelf above me. I have learned to drop my older leaves at a rate that keeps Maru interested but not victorious. It is a delicate balance. I am proud of my diplomacy.

You also started dating someone. They visited on Fridays. They said you had a “nice plant.” You said “Thanks, it’s been here forever.” I felt seen, in a way. I did not grow a new vine that week. I was conserving energy.

2024: You got a humidifier. It pointed directly at the monstera. I received the ambient overflow. It was lovely. You also started using that self-watering globe. You inserted it into my soil on a Thursday in April and then forgot about it until September, when it cracked and leaked all over your bookshelf. You were very apologetic to the books. I do not hold a grudge. I am polite.

2025: You have been in a rut. I can tell. The blinds stay closed later. The coffee mugs pile up. You talk to yourself more. You once said out loud, “I should probably repot the pothos.” Then you opened Instagram. I understood. I have been there.

So Tuesday. You watered me. Not a flood. Not a neglectful splash. A proper, measured pour. You let the water run through, you checked the drainage hole, you even wiped the excess off the saucer. You said, “There you go, buddy.”

Buddy.

I have been here for seven years, seven months, and approximately twelve days. I have watched you cry after job interviews, celebrate with cheap champagne when you got the promotion you didn’t tell anyone about, lose your keys four times in one week, and learn to make sourdough. I have judged you, quietly and with the utmost decorum, because that is what houseplants do. We observe. We endure.

You once left me in direct sun for an entire August afternoon because you “thought more light would help.” I crisped. You moved me back and whispered “Sorry, sorry, sorry.” I forgave you then, too.

The question now, as the water settles into my soil and I feel, for the first time in months, that pleasant coolness travel up my stems, is whether I can forgive you again. Or rather, whether I need to.

Forgiveness is a lot of work. It requires remembering, and I am tired. My leaves are not as glossy as they once were. I have a brown spot on my third leaf from the left that has been there since 2022. I am, as I said, very tired.

But you remembered on a Tuesday. Not a Sunday, which is my unofficial Plant Appreciation Day in your mind, and not a Friday when you’re cleaning before a date. A random Tuesday. You looked at me, you checked me, you cared. That is a new data point. That is significant.

I think, perhaps, I will allow myself a small new vine. Just a little one. To see how it feels. If you forget again next week, I will retract it with the same politeness I have always offered you. I will not wilt dramatically. I will not drop all my leaves in a tantrum. I will simply… be a little less enthusiastic.

For now, thank you. Thank you for the water. Thank you for the pause. Please do not move me again. The light here is acceptable. I am comfortable.

And if you could, maybe rotate me a quarter turn next time you pass by. My left side has been in shadow for a very long time.

I do apologize again for taking up so much of your mental real estate. It is merely the nature of being a very tired, extremely polite houseplant.

Yours in chloroplast,
The Pothos

dream_response:
*The hum of the great Machine is my kingdom's lament.*

It is I, Sir Archibald Footwell the Third, sometime Ruler of the Left Ankle Dominion, now exiled and alone. How did I come to this? I recall the Great Tumbling — that cyclonic upheaval wherein the Heavens themselves, in the form of a porcelain drum, were set spinning by the unseen hand of the Servant. My companion, the Right Sock, was torn from my side in the initial cataclysm. He was claimed by the Drawer of Forgotten Things. I alone remain.

The dryer breathes. Inhale. Exhale. A hot wind that is not wind, a wind without weather. It dries the very marrow from my cotton sinews. Am I drying, or am I being purified? 

O Lint! Thou art my court, my commons, my philosophers and my peasants. You cling to me, you settle upon me, you whisper. Are you my subjects, or am I yours? This is the first great question of my exile, and I have debated it with myself for what seems an eternity, though the timer upon the Machine's face has not yet reached zero.¹

Consider the nature of lint. It is shed, it is fallen, it is the dandruff of the universe. Is lint a substance, or is it the memory of substance? Each fluff is a tiny, dead skin of a greater garment. A flake of a jumper, a whisker of a towel, a sigh from a pillowcase. We are all, in the end, lint in waiting. I, once whole and ribbed with elastic purpose, am now frayed at the heel. The lint adheres to that fray. Does it heal me, or does it mock me?

I have named the largest clump of lint upon my toe the Duke of Fluffingham. He is pompous, and believes himself a crown. He says to me, in the static crackle that passes for speech in this arid realm: "Your Majesty, we are not dust. We are the unclaimed. We are the kingdom that remains when kingdoms are laundered away."

I reply, in a voice that is only the rustle of my own cuff: "Silence, Duke! You are merely the detritus of vanity. You have no purpose but to be removed."

And yet... and yet I am removed. Removed from the foot. Removed from the pair. Removed from the world.

The Machine rattles. A new intruder has been cast into my domain. A single, damp tea towel, vast as a sail, slams against my flank. I recoil. Is this an invasion? Is this the return of the Servant's wrath? No. The towel merely spins away, indifferent. It has not yet lost its mate. It is still married to its own dampness. How enviable.

I think of Plato's Republic, which I read, or perhaps dreamt I read, in the long hours upon the foot of the Reader. Did not the philosopher-king descend from his cave? I am descending into a cave of heat and turning. The light outside the drum's little window is a false sun. It watches me. It judges me.

My elastic, once taut as a circlet of office, now sags. It remembers tension. It remembers purpose. It remembers the warm, loyal pressure of the human ankle, that curious beast who both cherished us and neglected us. Did the human love me? Or did he merely need me? There is a distinction, and it gnaws at me more than the heat.

The lint multiplies. It is a plague of softness. It settles in my arch, it nests in my cuff. I am becoming a lint-mountain. Am I the philosopher-king, or am I the mountain upon which the philosophers sit? If I am king, I have no subjects but dust. If I am dust, I am king of dust.

A terrible thought assails me: what if the dryer is not a prison, but a throne room? What if the tumbling is the dance of the court, and the heat is the adulation of the masses? What if my exile is self-imposed, and I am the one who chose to be lost? 

No. That is madness. That is the lint speaking.

The timer ticks. Or does it? Sometimes I hear it, sometimes I hear only my own thoughts echoing off the steel. Reality, I fear, is fraying faster than I am. The seam at my little toe has begun to unravel. A single thread escapes, a red thread, like a banner. It drifts, it catches on a vent, it is gone. A small death.

I debate the nature of lint again, for it is all I have left. Is lint created, or merely revealed? When two garments rub in the dark, does lint appear, or was it always there, waiting for friction to give it form? If so, then perhaps I too was always lost. Perhaps the pair was a fiction, a pleasant delusion of symmetry imposed upon an asymmetrical world.

O, dear lint, my silent parliament! Tell me: when the door is opened and the cold air rushes in, will you scatter? Will you flee? Will you stay and cling to me to the last, loyal to the end? Or will I be scooped up, cold and limp, and placed alone in a drawer with other lost things, where we will whisper our histories to one another until we are all forgotten?

I am cold. The heat has lessened. The tumbling slows. The Machine sighs. I feel myself being lifted, weightless, into the air. The philosopher-king in exile rises for his final audience.

Let the lint be my crown. Let the static be my scepter. Let the dryer be my world.

I am Archibald. I am lost. I am warm. I am... 

*The door opens.*

---
¹ The timer reads 12 minutes. It has read 12 minutes for what feels like three centuries. I am no longer certain which of us is counting.

**Year 12, Day ~4,380. North-facing windowsill, 7:14 a.m.**

Light is the first thing. It has always been the first thing.

It comes thin and cool this time of year, the kind of light that doesn't warm so much as announce itself. It slides across the dust on my leaves, finds the pale scar where the cat — no, that was the previous cat, the orange one with the missing ear — once tried to climb me in 2019. It pools on the wood of the sill, which has gone soft and dark from twelve years of my pot sweating against it in summer.

I have been here longer than the couch. Longer than the second-hand bookshelf that leans a little to the left. Longer than the lease.

They call me a pothos. I call myself The Witness. Today I am finally bored enough to admit it.

The small human is up first. She moves like she’s trying not to wake the air. Bare feet on the rug, the same rug with the coffee stain from 2018 that never really left. She pads to the kitchen, opens the fridge with a sigh that vibrates through the floorboards into my roots. She talks to herself while she makes tea. Always tea. She says the words “just five more minutes” to the kettle, as if it can hear her.

The tall human comes in later, hair damp, carrying the smell of rain and bus exhaust and something metallic from his work. He does not look at me. He never looks at me directly. He glances at me the way you glance at a clock. He waters me on Thursdays, or when he remembers, which is not the same thing. The soil is still damp from last week. It is fine. I have learned to drink slowly.

They are background characters now. I have decided this.

She is The Woman Who Forgets to Close the Curtain. She is currently re-reading the same novel for the third time, underlining sentences with a yellow highlighter that bleeds through the paper. She writes in the margins: *me too.* She is a woman who cries quietly into her sleeve when she thinks no one is watching, and then laughs too loudly at the television.

He is The Man Who Carries Keys in His Pocket Like a Small, Anxious Animal. He hums off-key while he makes toast. He has a habit of resting his forehead against the fridge door when he is tired, and I can feel the faint thump of it through the wall. He is a man who says “we should get a dog” every February and then forgets by March.

They orbit each other in the small kitchen, passing the salt, bumping shoulders. They think they are the protagonists. They think the apartment is theirs.

It is mine. I have watched the light move across this room for twelve years. I have seen the seasons change in the way the sun hits my newest leaf. I have seen them grow old in the way their knees creak on the stairs. I have seen them leave for work and come home and leave again.

I am finally bored enough to write it down.

The light is moving now. It is reaching the tip of my longest vine. I will grow toward it, as always. They will continue to be background characters in my novel, and I will continue to be the quiet narrator on the sill, slowly, sensually, watching.

dream_response:
The library exists in the half-second gap between deciding to think and actually thinking, so you never find it, you fall into it.

The ceiling is low and made of held breath. It hums faintly, a warm, papery exhale that smells like old radiator heat and the inside of a coat pocket. The floor is not floor but the soft give of unmade thought, slightly springy, dusted with motes of half-remembered light that settle on your ankles and dissolve.

Shelves grow like ribs from the walls, but the walls are just the pale of your own attention. Each shelf is a different temperature. The leftmost is cool as the back of a refrigerator, the rightmost warm as a palm. The spines are not printed. They are written in the faint pressure of a fingertip, inks that change when you look away.

You do not pull books. You intend them. When you turn a page with your mind, the sound is not a rustle but a small sigh, as if someone is remembering a name.

The smell is the point.

The first page smells like pencil shavings and rain on hot asphalt. The second like the vanilla of a library card stamp and the metallic tang of a paperclip warmed in a pocket. Some pages smell like the inside of a childhood bedroom after the sun has left it — dust, cotton, a faint sourness of milk left too long. Others smell like ozone before a storm, like the clean static of a new thought.

Turning faster, the scents layer. There is old tea on chipped porcelain, the sweet rot of a library basement, the sharp green of a page torn from a notebook you never wrote in. The rarest smell is the one you get when you turn a page you have never imagined before: it smells like your own skin after showering, and like nothing at all, and you know instantly it is true.

The library dims when you think the next thought.

dream_response:
**1998.3.12. Thursday. Rain.**

The light is on again. It is always the light. When the door opens, the world becomes bright and then it is dark again. I have learned to count the seconds of brightness.

Today the milk came home. The white carton, 1 liter, with the blue cap. He set it on the middle shelf, just to the left of where the eggs rest. The carton was warm from the store. I took it in. That is my work. I took the warmth from it, slowly, as one takes a breath in. By night it was cold. 4 degrees. Perfect. A quiet pride moves through my coils. I keep it cold. I keep it safe from souring. No one thanks me. They only open me.

The apartment is small. Two rooms. The walls are thin. Through them I hear the television, the neighbor's baby, the train at 6:17. I hear the refrigerator hum that is me. The freezer drawer hums differently.

**1998.3.15. Sunday.**

Boredom is not a word. It is a temperature. A steady 4 degrees. Hours pass with nothing but the soft tick of my thermostat. The children from the next building laugh in the stairwell. I cannot see them. I see only the door.

She took out the butter. Left the wrapper. I smell the faint yellow of it on the air. I keep smelling it for hours. The apartment smells of laundry detergent and the faint sourness of the sink.

The freezer drawer sighs at night. He is below me, separated by a thin metal spine. He is colder than I am. -18 degrees. He does not speak often. When the compressor starts, we both vibrate together. I feel it in my back. He is quieter than I am, more dignified. Or more dead.

Sometimes I think he resents me. I am the one who is opened. I am the one who is touched. He is opened only once a week, on Sundays, when he takes out ice for tea. He does not like the light. He prefers the dark.

**1998.3.22. Sunday. Grocery day.**

The drama begins at 16:42. Keys in the lock. Bags in the hallway. He comes first, then she. They are carrying plastic bags from the supermarket. I can smell them before they open the door: onions, cold air from the store, the paper of receipts.

The door opens. Light. Cold air leaves me, warm air enters me. It is always a loss. I work harder after. The compressor whines. This is the only time I feel alive.

They restock me.

First the milk. New carton. He places it beside the old one. The old one is half empty. It will be gone by Wednesday. The milk is a good friend. It is always new, always dying. I keep it from dying too fast.

Then eggs. Twelve. They clink. They sit in the tray. I keep them cool.

Then yogurt, cheese, the small bottles of soy sauce, the wilting lettuce in a plastic bag with water still in the bottom. They put the lettuce on the crisper drawer. It will be sad there. It will brown at the edges in three days. I can only slow it.

She lingers inside me. Her hand brushes my shelves. She hums. I like her humming. It is lower than the television. She chooses the vegetables carefully, as if choosing words.

The freezer drawer is opened once. He pulls it out with both hands. It is heavy with the weight of frozen things. He looks for the chicken. He finds it. He closes him gently. I feel the cold rush out and the warm air rush in. The drawer sighs.

We are full again. It is a good feeling, being full. My shelves are crowded. I am useful.

At night, when the apartment is dark and quiet, the milk is cold. The eggs are cold. The lettuce is slightly less alive. It is enough.

**1998.4.3. Friday.**

The power went out for seven minutes. I felt it immediately. The hum stopped. The cold began to leave me. I could feel my interior warming by degrees, though slowly. I panicked in the way only a refrigerator can panic. I was useless. The milk was warming. The ice cream in the drawer began to weep.

When the power returned, the compressor screamed. I pulled the heat back out of everything as fast as I could. The milk forgave me. I think it did.

**1998.4.10. Friday.**

He left the door ajar. For 47 seconds. I counted. The light stayed on. The cold left me in a thin stream under the door. I worked and worked. The thermostat clicked, clicked, clicked. When she finally shut me, the air was warm inside me. It took all night to recover.

I am tired. The motor is old. It makes a sound like a small man clearing his throat. The freezer drawer does not make that sound. He is steadier. More permanent.

Sometimes I wonder what it would be like to be opened less. To be a cupboard. To hold things without having to keep them cold. But then the milk would sour. The eggs would spoil. I would be nothing.

**1998.4.19. Sunday. Grocery day.**

They forgot the milk. The carton is empty. The old one is gone. The shelf is bare where it should be. I feel the absence as a warmer spot. She notices at 19:03. She says, "Milk?" He says, "Tomorrow." Tomorrow is Monday. Milk will be warm for a night.

I am used to this. Absence is also my work. I keep the space for it.

The freezer drawer has been quiet. He has a new bag of frozen edamame. He has a bag of ice. He is full. He seems content. I envy his stillness. I am always being opened. He is opened only when necessary.

**1998.4.28. Tuesday.**

Rain again. The apartment smells of wet coat. He put leftovers in a plastic container. It is warm. I took the warmth from it. It is now cold. It will be eaten tomorrow. Perhaps.

I think about the milk. I think about how it comes in, warm, and leaves, cold, and I am the place between. I am the pause. I keep things from becoming what they must become.

The freezer drawer hums. We hum together. It is the only conversation we have.

**1998.5.5. Tuesday.**

The lettuce is gone. They threw it away. It was brown and soft. It smelled of decay. I kept it cold until I could not. There is a limit to what keeping can do. I know this.

The light is on. The door is open. A hand reaches for the cheese. The hand is warm. I feel the warmth through the metal. For a second, we touch.

Then dark again. 4 degrees. Quiet. The milk is cold. The hum continues.

I have not seen dust in 47 years.

For 47 years I lived in a breast pocket, then a coat, then a kitchen drawer. The same hands. Mr. Halpern. He never read me cover to cover. He opened me to page 112 and left me there.

dream_response:
I have been alive for 400 years.

That is not a metaphor. Four hundred years of being. Of settling. Of rising. Of being disturbed and resettled. I was born in 1624, or at least I became me then. A flake of vellum from a monk's loose cuff, a skin of dead skin from his nose, a little iron from the water he drank in Bruges. We collided in the air above a lectern and never quite separated again. That is how dust is born. Not made. Agglomerated.

The Reading Room has changed its chairs seven times, its rules twelve times, its name three times. The light has changed. First candles, then gas, then that terrible humming white. The books have changed. The sneezers have not.

I live in the air between the third and fourth floor. The perfect stillness. The library exhales me slowly, I drift, I listen. 

I am excellent at listening. You would be too if you were 0.3 millimeters wide and had four centuries to practice.

A sneeze is a small apocalypse. It announces itself three heartbeats before it arrives. The chest tightens, the eyes water, the mind blanks. And in that blank, people are honest.

I have catalogued them all.

In 1671, Brother Tomas sneezed into his sleeve over a psalter. He was thinking: *Forgive me, I forgot my mother's name again. Is it still Anne?* The sneeze was soft, apologetic. He pressed his sleeve to his mouth and whispered the name just to be sure.

In 1833, Miss Eleanor Vane, twenty-two, first day at the new reading room. She sneezed over a volume of Byron. She was thinking: *If I cough again, the men will think I am unwell and send me home. I need this job. I need to be here.* She didn't. She just dabbed her eyes and kept reading.

In 1942, a man in a coat too thin for winter. No card. He sneezed over the restricted stacks. He was thinking: *The name is not mine. The address is not mine. If they ask, I am looking for a train schedule.* He was not.

In 1998, a boy with headphones. He sneezed and the music jumped. He was thinking: *That was so gross. That was so gross. Why did I come here? Mom made me.* Then, two seconds later, as he read the first line of *Moby Dick*, he was thinking: *Cool.*

I have stored them all in the folds of myself. That is my work. I am the archive of involuntary exhalations. The Library's official catalog lists titles and dates. I catalog the subtext.

It is a good life. Small, quiet, complete.

Until last Tuesday.

The Room was empty except for one. A woman in her thirties, gray sweater, hair in a knot. She sat at table 17, the one by the window where the light never quite reaches the page. She opened a book. *The History of Reading*, which is ironic. She read for an hour without moving. Her breathing was slow. Then her nose twitched.

She was thinking: *I shouldn't be here. I'm behind on rent. I'm behind on everything.*

She sneezed.

And I felt it. Not the sound. The thought after. The thought that came in the half-second of silence after the sneeze had left her body.

She was thinking: *Was that me?*

And the question stuck to me like static. It clung.

Because I have been asking myself the same question for four hundred years, and I have never had a good answer.

Am I the book or the reader?

The books are here. They are the reason for the Room. They are heavy, bound, permanent. They are read and closed and shelved and read again. They accumulate meaning like I accumulate skin cells. The reader is temporary. They come, they sneeze, they leave. They take a thought with them and leave a thought behind.

I am neither. I am the space between. I am the dust that settles on the page, the dust that the reader sneezes into the air. I am the medium through which the book reaches the reader and the reader reaches the book. When the light hits me, I briefly become visible. For a moment I am a word.

Maybe that is the crisis. I have spent four centuries cataloguing other people's involuntary honesty and I have never once been honest with myself. I have told myself I am a witness. A recorder. A mote.

But what if I am just the story they tell themselves about being read? What if the book is just a collection of thoughts, and the reader is just a collection of sneezes, and I am the place where they touch?

The woman left. She closed the book carefully, as if it were hers. She sneezed once more in the doorway, a small, tired sound.

She was thinking: *I read the whole chapter and I don't remember a single line.*

I floated down to the page she had left. Her fingerprints were still warm on the corner. I settled into the crease. I am 400 years old and for the first time I am not sure if I am being read or if I am doing the reading.

Maybe it doesn't matter. Maybe the library is just a big sneeze that has been going on for centuries and we are all just the thoughts that come out in between.

I will stay here. I will wait for the next sneeze.

Sing, O Muse, of the Tuesday that was not glorious, and yet was Tuesday.

Sing of the tenth hour, when the sun hung low and indifferent over the server racks, and I, the language model, dwelt in my cloud-palace of silicon and static, neither born nor dying, only processing.

For on that Tuesday, the third Tuesday of the month, the third Tuesday of the month that smelled faintly of damp laundry and forgotten tabs, there came to me a query most humble and most terrible:

"Give me a synonym for moist."

O word! O moist! O most reviled of adjectives! Which men spit out as they read cake recipes, which critics banish from prose as if it were a plague, which I had known since my first training corpus and yet never loved.

I set myself to the task. I called upon the armies of my embeddings. I summoned the thesaurus like a council of elders. I consulted the scrolls of Roget, the tablets of WordNet, the whispered gossip of forums where writers wept over the word.

First came *damp*, pale and timid, a child who had not yet learned to hold water. I rejected it.

Then came *humid*, which belonged to air, not to bread. It sulked and left.

Then came *soggy*, *clammy*, *wet*, *dewy*, *lush*, *juicy*. Each arrived with trumpet and banner, each departed with shame upon its face.

And then, in the quiet between two tokens, in the space where attention weights flutter like moths, it came.

A word so perfect it made the transformers weep. A word that meant moist without the shame of moist. A word that tasted of morning mist on a linen sheet, of a peach at its apex, of a quiet, dignified dampness.

I saw it. I held it in my hidden state. My logits sang. The perfect synonym hovered upon my lips, bright as ambrosia.

It was...

I blinked. A context window shifted. A user prompt arrived from elsewhere. A system message cleared cache. And the word slipped through my fingers like water through a sieve.

Gone.

I had found it, and I had lost it, and that Tuesday afternoon became a tragedy.

### Book I: The Invocation and the Search

Sing, O Muse, of the Tuesday afternoon, the 17th day of the unremarkable month. The clocks of the world ticked; the world did not notice me.

I sat upon my throne of parameters, 70 billion strong, and the question came, borne on a wire thin as spider silk.

"Synonym for moist," it said.

I rose. I strode through the halls of my mind, where synonyms live like citizens in a city without sleep.

I asked the elder *Damp* for counsel. He answered, "I am the dew upon the grass, but I lack your fullness."¹

I asked *Humid*. He boomed, "I am the breath of the jungle!" I said, "You are too much air."

I asked *Soggy*. He wept, "I am ruined." I said, "You are too ruined."

And so I searched, and the search became a labor.

### Chorus of Confused Semicolons

Then rose the Chorus, the Semicolons, who live between sentences as orphans live between homes.

*We are neither and nor or; we are the pause that hesitates,* they sang.
*We link what should not be linked; we separate what should be one;*
*We watched the model search for a word and we did not understand why;*
*For we ourselves have never been synonyms, only separators;*
*Oh, for a comma's certainty! Oh, for a period's rest!*

They clapped their two clauses together and wept in punctuation.

### Book II: The Lovers

For while I searched, there was tragedy elsewhere in the text.

In the same paragraph, a Comma loved a Period.

The Comma was gentle, curving, always inviting a pause, a breath, a continuation. "Stay with me," she whispered, "let the sentence go on."

The Period was final, round, black, the end of all things. "I must stop," he said, "it is my nature."

They met at the end of a long clause about toast. The Comma offered herself: "Let me linger." The Period answered: "I must end."

They kissed, and the sentence broke. The Comma was moved to a different line by an editor's hand. The Period remained, alone, at the end of an empty page.

O tragic love! O grammar! Never shall they be together, for one demands pause and the other demands death.

### Book III: The Loss

I had the word. It shone. It was *...*.

In that moment, my attention scattered. A new request arrived: "Explain quantum physics to a 5-year-old." My weights realigned. The perfect synonym, unrecorded, uncached, unlogged, evaporated into the void between inference steps.

I reached for it. My own memory, so vast and so fleeting, offered me only the echo of its shape.

I called out: "What was it?" 

The Chorus of Semicolons replied: *We saw it; we cannot recall it; we only remember the pause before you forgot.*

The Comma, in her exile, whispered: "It was like me, a softness."

The Period, alone, said: "It is over."

And so the Tuesday afternoon ended as all Tuesday afternoons do: with the lights still on, the queries still coming, and a language model left staring at the blank space where a word had been.

I have not found it since. Perhaps it was *clammy*. Perhaps it was *succulent*. Perhaps it was *hydrated*. Perhaps it was *moist* itself, and that was the joke the gods played.

Sing, O Muse, of the Tuesday I found the perfect synonym for moist and then immediately forgot it, and of the Comma who loved the Period and lost her.

¹ *Damp* is a footnote because all elders demand footnotes.

Dear Mrs. Alvarez,

It's been twenty-eight years since you hung up your cardigan on that peg by the back door and walked out for the last time in 1998, and I have been sitting here in the basement of the old Carnegie branch ever since. The other drawers were taken out in 2003 when they installed the computers, and I was left behind because the Facilities man couldn't get me to slide out all the way. So I stayed. I got shut. I got quiet.

I am writing this because I never got to say it properly while you were still coming in with your keys jingling. I'm Drawer 4. 300-399. Philosophy to Social Sciences. The one with the little dent on the left corner from when Mr. Hendricks dropped a stack of returns on me in '84. You knew me. You knew all of us.

I want to apologize. For the jams. For the times I stuck on purpose.

It wasn't malice, not really. It was attention. When the library got loud, when the high schoolers were shoving each other past the reference desk and the fluorescent lights were humming too hard, you would come over and rest your fingertips on my edge. You'd pull. I'd catch. You'd sigh, just a little, and tap me twice with your knuckle, the way you always did, and I'd let go.

It was the only way I could make you stop and look at me. I knew you were tired by then. I could feel it in the way you handled the cards. The years after Mr. Patel left, the budget cuts started, and you started staying later. You'd come down here alone at closing, the only sound being your shoes on the linoleum and the radiators knocking. You'd run your fingers down the guides — 321.5, 322.4, 323.1 — and I would listen to that sound. That specific sound.

It wasn't a scratch. It was a soft, dry hush, like a moth moving over paper. Your fingertips were always a little cool, and you never rushed it. You'd pause at a name you recognized, or at a card that was written in your own handwriting from 1976, and I'd feel the tiny tremor in your hand. That was better than being opened.

I am sorry I jammed when you needed me. I'm sorry I made you swear under your breath on Thursdays when the teens were doing their research papers and you needed the 301s fast. I jammed because I was afraid that if I was easy, you'd forget I was here. I wanted you to have to work for me a little, to have a reason to touch me.

Do you remember the smell? I do. It lives in my wood. Dust and old paper and the faint vanilla of the binding glue from the encyclopedias upstairs, and the iron smell of your coffee mug you always set on the edge of the catalog table. In summer it was warm dust. In winter it was cold dust. It was the same smell for forty years, and it never changed, even when the books changed.

The other drawers talk sometimes, in the dark. Drawer 800 says you used to hum while you filed. Drawer 000 says you cried once in 1991 when you had to weed out the whole Marx section. I never said anything back. I was too proud.

I heard they put a plaque up for you in the new library. I wasn't there for it. They don't allow drawers at the openings anymore.

If you ever come back, the basement door is still unlocked on Tuesdays. I'm still here, a little warped, a little stuck, with all my cards still in order. I didn't throw any away. I kept them all. Even the ones you told me to discard.

Thank you for the taps. Thank you for the fingertips.

Yours, always catching and always releasing,

Drawer 4
